unit.can_do_en: join a coffee break and accept a sauna invitation.

brief.situation_en: Maria and her colleagues Ville and Aino.

judge.reason: Tuuk sä = Tuletko sinä; same question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Yes, I'm coming. Is there pulla?

judge.reason: Joo/kyllä, mä tuun/minä tulen, onks/onko are only register differences.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: I baked them yesterday. Help yourselves!

judge.reason: Mä/minä only register difference; content is the same.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Tosi hyviä! Juotteks te aina näin paljon kahvia?
lines.text_kirja: Todella hyviä! Juotteko te aina näin paljon kahvia?
lines.gloss_en: Really good! Do you always drink this much coffee?

judge.reason: Tosi/todella and juotteks/juotteko are register variants.

puhe.text: Tosi hyviä! Juotteks te aina näin paljon kahvia?

kirja.text: Todella hyviä! Juotteko te aina näin paljon kahvia?

lines.speaker: Ville
lines.text_puhe: Joo. Suomalaiset juo eniten kahvia maailmas.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä. Suomalaiset juovat eniten kahvia maailmassa.
lines.gloss_en: Yes. Finns drink the most coffee in the world.

judge.reason: Juo/juovat and maailmas/maailmassa are register differences; same claim.

puhe.text: Joo. Suomalaiset juo eniten kahvia maailmas.

kirja.text: Kyllä. Suomalaiset juovat eniten kahvia maailmassa.

judge.reason: Sit/sitten and mäkin/minäkin are register variants.
Santsia is spoken for 'more/seconds', equal to lisää.

forms.why_en: This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Tulet (you come) with the question ending -ko: tuletko. Speech says tuuksä, glued to sä.
Speech shortens sinä to sä. Books write sinä.
Joo is the everyday spoken yes. Books write kyllä.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Adds -en for 'I': tulla becomes tulen. Speech says tuun.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: On with -ko to ask a question. Speech often says -ks: onks.
Adds -a for some pulla: pullaa. Pulla is a sweet Finnish bun.
The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
Tuoda changes to toi for something that already happened. It looks like toi (that) in speech.
Plural 'some' takes -ja: korvapuusti becomes korvapuusteja, i turning into e.
Leipoa changes to leivo- with -i- for the past and -n for 'I': leivoin.
Ne means they, for things. Speech also uses it for people.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -kaa to tell more than one person: ottakaa, 'take'.
Books write todella. In speech people use tosi, 'really', instead.
Hyvä becomes hyviä when talking about several things, here the buns.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person plural, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Juotte (you all drink) with the question ending -ko: juotteko. Speech says juotteks.
Te is 'you' when you talk to more than one person. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The partitive adds -a for 'some': kahvia. Here speech says it the same way.
Adds -t for more than one: suomalainen becomes suomalaiset.
Books add -vat for 'they': juovat. Speech uses the he or she form: juo.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -ssa for 'in': maailma becomes maailmassa. Speech shortens -ssa to -s: maailmassa becomes maailmas.
Speech shortens sitten to sit. Books write sitten.
Minä with -kin, 'too': minäkin. Speech shortens it to mäkin.
Opetella, to learn, with -n for 'I': opettelen.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Books write lisää. Speech often says santsia, mostly about more food.
